title: How to Improve Indoor Air Quality in Winter
h1: Winter Indoor Air Quality Tips for a Healthier Home
description: Closed windows and a running furnace can make winter air stale and dusty. These practical tips cover filters, ventilation, humidity, furnace safety and more.
quick_answer: To improve indoor air quality in winter, change your furnace filter, get the furnace checked before heavy use, ventilate briefly every day, run kitchen and bath exhaust fans, keep humidity in a comfortable range, and test your carbon monoxide alarms. In Southern California, it also helps to plan for fireplace smoke and late-season Santa Ana winds.
body:
Winter in San Diego and Orange County is mild by most standards, but inland nights still get cold enough to keep the heat running and the windows shut. That's when indoor air quality tends to slip. The furnace stirs up dust that's been sitting all summer, cooking and showers add moisture with nowhere to go, and the house just doesn't get much fresh air.

The fixes are mostly simple. Here's what makes the biggest difference.

Why does indoor air get worse in winter?

A few things happen at once when the weather cools:

  • Less fresh air. Windows and doors stay closed, so cooking odors, dust and everyday pollutants build up.
  • The first furnace start. A furnace that's sat idle for months can burn off dust and blow it through the ducts the first few times it runs.
  • More time indoors. More cooking, more candles, more people and pets in the same rooms.
  • Fireplaces. Wood fires on cool evenings add smoke and fine particles inside.

Start with the furnace and filter

Your heating system moves air through the whole house, so it's the best place to start.

Change the filter before the season

Put a fresh filter in before you turn the heat on for the year, then check it monthly. In many local homes, the filter is in a hallway return grille, a hall closet or right at the furnace in the garage or attic. A clean pleated filter catches more dust and keeps airflow strong.

Get a furnace tune-up

A yearly check-up cleans the burners and blower, confirms the system is venting correctly, and catches cracked parts or loose connections before they become a problem. Our heating technicians can do this before the cold nights arrive. Gas valves, burners and electrical parts should always be left to a professional.

How do you keep fresh air coming in when it's cold?

You don't have to freeze to ventilate. A few habits keep stale air from building up:

  1. Open a couple of windows for 10 to 15 minutes on the warmest part of the day.
  2. Run the range hood every time you cook, especially with a gas stove.
  3. Run bathroom exhaust fans during showers and for a while after.
  4. Make sure the dryer vents outdoors and isn't clogged with lint.

On smoky or very windy days, skip the open windows and rely on your filtered system instead.

What about humidity?

Humidity in winter is a balancing act. Too dry and your skin, eyes and sinuses feel it. Too damp and you get window condensation, musty smells and mold.

Coastal homes usually have plenty of moisture, and showers and cooking can push it higher. Inland homes can get dry when the heat runs a lot or when Santa Ana winds blow through. An inexpensive hygrometer tells you where your home actually sits, so you know whether you need a humidifier, a dehumidifier or neither.

Is winter fire and furnace safety part of air quality?

Yes, and it's the most important part. Any fuel-burning appliance can produce carbon monoxide if something goes wrong.

  • Test your carbon monoxide alarms and replace batteries before the heating season. You want one on every level and near sleeping areas.
  • Never use a gas oven, grill or outdoor heater to warm the house.
  • Have the fireplace and chimney inspected if you use them, and open the damper before lighting a fire.

If a CO alarm goes off, get everyone out of the house and call 911. If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside. Don't flip switches or try to find the leak yourself.

What else helps?

  • Clean before the season. Dust vents, returns and baseboards so the furnace isn't spreading last season's dust.
  • Use an air purifier. A portable HEPA unit in the bedroom helps, especially for allergy sufferers or on smoky evenings.
  • Consider whole-home upgrades. Media filters, UV lights and humidity control can be added to your existing system. See our indoor air quality options.
  • Look at your ducts. If you see dust blowing from vents or notice a burning-dust smell that doesn't go away after the first few runs, the ducts may need cleaning or repair.
faqs: Why does my house smell like burning dust when I turn on the heat?

Dust settles on the furnace's heat exchanger and burners over the warm months. The first few times the heat runs, it burns off. That's normal for a short time. If the smell lasts more than a day, turn the system off and call for service. If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside.
How often should I change my furnace filter in winter?
Check it monthly during the heating season and replace it when it looks dirty. Homes with pets, allergies or fireplace use usually need more frequent changes.
Should I run a humidifier in winter in Southern California?
Only if your home is actually dry. Many coastal homes have enough moisture already. Use a hygrometer to check before adding a humidifier, since too much moisture can lead to condensation and mold.
Do I need a carbon monoxide detector if I have a gas furnace?
Yes. Any home with a gas furnace, water heater, stove, fireplace or attached garage should have working carbon monoxide alarms on each level and near bedrooms. Test them before the heating season.
